headline: Microsoft surges on AI earnings beat last night while PLS slides 2% at today's ASX close — and OpenAI declares the "AGI era" has arrived.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft jumped last night after reporting strong AI-driven growth — one headline cited a 15% surge on earnings that beat expectations. The market is rewarding Microsoft's dominant position in enterprise AI through Azure and Copilot. This is the star performer in the portfolio right now, up 15% overall.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI bounced +1.6% at today's ASX close, likely riding the wave of excitement around this week's major AI model launches (GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash) and Microsoft's strong result. Still underwater overall (-13%), but sentiment is improving.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google gained last night after a US court rejected attempts to break up its ad-tech business. That removes a major regulatory overhang. Google also launched Gemini 3.8 Flash this week, keeping it competitive in the AI race.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS fell 2.1% at today's close as broad selling pressure hit ASX lithium stocks. No company-specific news drove it — the whole lithium sector faced headwinds today. PLS remains the portfolio's weakest position, down nearly 25% overall.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS ticked up 0.4% today, reflecting last night's solid US session — the S&P 500 rose 1.1% and NASDAQ climbed 1.4%, driven largely by big tech strength.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG nudged up 0.2% today — a quiet, steady session. This diversified fund just does its thing regardless of daily noise, which is exactly what you want from it.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE edged up slightly today. Emerging markets are ticking along — no major catalyst, just quiet positive movement. The AUD strengthening a touch (now above 72 US cents) is worth watching, as it slightly reduces the AUD value of overseas-denominated assets.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two dipped about 1% last night. Rockstar broke its silence on 'heartbreaking' GTA VI leaks — the news kept the stock in focus but didn't provide a positive catalyst. The long-term bull case still rests on GTA VI delivering when it ships.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Strong AI earnings — long-term story firing
watch_today.detail: Microsoft surged last night on strong AI-driven revenue growth, with some reports citing a 15% jump on the earnings result. As a long-term holder, this is exactly the kind of validation you want to see — Azure AI adoption is clearly accelerating. Sit tight and let it compound.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium selling pressure continues — hold your nerve
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped 2.1% today as the whole ASX lithium sector faced broad selling. PLS is now down nearly 25% on your cost base. The long-term lithium demand story (EVs, energy storage) remains intact — analysts still see demand growth supporting prices — but the short-term pain is real. No structural reason to sell; this is a sector caught in a wait-and-see phase.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI excitement building — still underwater though
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF bounced 1.6% today off the back of a massive week in AI news — GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and strong MSFT earnings. The AI theme is very much alive. You're still down 13% overall on this position, but the tailwinds are strengthening. Hold and let the theme play out.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA VI leaks in the news — watch but don't panic
watch_today.detail: Rockstar addressed 'heartbreaking' GTA VI leaks this week, keeping Take-Two in the headlines. The stock slipped about 1% last night. Your position is down 7.8% overall — the investment thesis is entirely tied to GTA VI's eventual release. Nothing has changed structurally; this is a long wait-and-hold situation.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike risk rising — watch your mortgage/cash
watch_today.detail: The Australian dollar pushed above 72 US cents today as markets increasingly price in an RBA rate hike. Fresh data shows productivity is at its worst level since 2007, and the RBA flagged that rising rents are keeping inflation sticky. If you have a variable-rate mortgage or cash savings, a rate hike would bite on borrowing and help on deposits. No portfolio action needed, but worth knowing.

watch_today.title: US jobs data (NFP) out tonight — could move markets
watch_today.detail: US Non-Farm Payrolls (the monthly jobs report — a key measure of economic health) drops tonight US time. A strong number could push the Fed to keep rates higher for longer; a weak number could signal rate cuts ahead. Either way it will likely move the S&P 500 and NASDAQ when US markets open at 11:30 PM AEST. Your VTS and US holdings may react tomorrow.

world.summary: The Middle East is escalating again with Iran striking Kuwait and renewed US airstrikes, Trump is pushing voting restriction battles to the Supreme Court with midterms looming, and the Iran conflict is now being priced by global insurers for the first time.

stories.title: Iran strikes Kuwait as US-Iran conflict escalates — Trump says it 'won't last long'
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has struck Kuwait in a significant escalation of the ongoing US-Iran conflict, while the Trump administration conducted renewed US airstrikes against Iranian targets. Trump publicly said the campaign 'won't last long' — but markets and insurers aren't so sure. Oil prices (currently around $90.76/barrel) remain elevated, and global shipping and insurance costs are climbing. For everyday Australians, a prolonged Middle East conflict means higher petrol prices and broader cost-of-living pressure.

stories.title: BBC asks: how could the US-Iran conflict end?
stories.why_it_matters: With US and Iranian forces exchanging strikes, analysts are openly asking how and when this ends. The BBC outlines scenarios ranging from a negotiated ceasefire to a broader regional war drawing in Saudi Arabia and Israel. There's no obvious off-ramp right now — both sides have domestic political reasons to appear tough. The longer it drags on, the bigger the risk to global oil supply routes through the Persian Gulf, which Australia depends on.

stories.title: Lloyd's of London puts a price on the Iran conflict for the first time
stories.why_it_matters: Lloyd's of London — the world's leading insurance marketplace — has for the first time formally quantified its exposure to the US-Iran conflict and warned of a tougher year ahead for the industry. When Lloyd's flags rising war-risk costs, it flows through to higher shipping insurance premiums globally, which ultimately raises prices on imported goods. It's also a signal that institutional money is taking this conflict seriously as a lasting economic risk, not a short-term flare-up.

stories.title: Trump appeals to Supreme Court to restrict mail-in voting ahead of US midterms
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration has filed an urgent appeal with the Supreme Court to implement new rules restricting who can vote by mail, with US midterm elections fast approaching. The administration wants the court to allow USPS (postal service) mail-in ballot restrictions to take effect now, before lower courts have fully ruled. This is a major voting rights battle — if the Supreme Court sides with Trump, it could significantly reduce mail-in voting access in key states ahead of the midterms, reshaping the political landscape and market expectations around the election outcome.

markets.summary: Last night was a strong night for US markets — the S&P 500 rose 1.1% and the NASDAQ jumped 1.4%, driven by big tech earnings strength, particularly Microsoft. The ASX had a flat-to-slightly-negative day, slipping 0.16%. Gold hit $4,511 and the Aussie dollar is up solidly above 72 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Quiet, slightly negative session today. The index held above 9,000 which is a psychologically important level.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Solid gain last night, lifted by big tech — particularly Microsoft's AI earnings beat.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Strong night last night for tech stocks. AI enthusiasm and Microsoft earnings drove the gains.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar climbed above 72 US cents today as markets increasingly expect the RBA to raise interest rates. A stronger AUD slightly reduces the AUD value of your US holdings (MSFT, GOOG, TTWO).

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Gold continues to push higher — at $4,511/oz it's near historic highs, likely driven by Middle East uncertainty and inflation concerns.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil dipped slightly despite the Iran-Kuwait escalation — markets may be pricing in Trump's 'won't last long' comments. Still elevated at ~$90/barrel.

politics.summary: The big domestic story today is the RBA and inflation — fresh data shows Australia's productivity is at its worst level since 2007, and the RBA has flagged that soaring rents are keeping inflation stubbornly high. Markets are now firmly pricing in a rate hike, and the Aussie dollar is responding.

stories.title: RBA warns rents are keeping inflation high — rate hike bets surge
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has publicly flagged that rising rents across the country are a major driver of persistent inflation — making it harder for them to bring inflation down without raising rates. With rent prices still climbing in cities like Sydney, Brisbane, and the Gold Coast, the RBA faces a tough call. Markets have now sharply increased their bets on a rate hike, which pushed the AUD up to 0.7207 today. If you have a variable-rate mortgage, this is one to watch closely.

stories.title: Australia's productivity hits worst level since 2007 — bad news for the RBA's inflation fight
stories.why_it_matters: New figures show Australian productivity — how much output workers produce per hour — has fallen to its lowest point since 2007, worse than the levels seen during the GFC lead-up. Low productivity is inflationary because businesses pay more per unit of work, pushing up prices. This data makes the RBA's job harder: they can't cut rates to stimulate growth without risking inflation blowing out further. The political heat on Labor is rising, with commentators arguing the government's economic management is compounding the problem.

stories.title: Don't blame the RBA for Labor's political incompetence — The Australian
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian's opinion columnists are squarely blaming the Albanese Labor government — not the Reserve Bank — for Australia's economic struggles, pointing to poor productivity policy and wage decisions that have made inflation harder to tame. This reflects a broader political narrative building ahead of the next election cycle: that Labor inherited a manageable situation and made it worse. The RBA is increasingly caught in the crossfire between economic reality and political blame-shifting.

ai.summary: This week has been the biggest in AI news for years. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra and declared the 'AGI era' has arrived, Google fired back with Gemini 3.8 Flash, and major AI services suffered a simultaneous outage. All the big players moved at once — and regulators worldwide are scrambling to keep up.

stories.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra and declares the 'AGI era' has arrived
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Astra — its most powerful model yet — and boldly declared this marks the beginning of the 'AGI era' (AGI stands for Artificial General Intelligence, meaning AI that can perform any intellectual task a human can). The model comes with warnings about its advanced cyber capabilities, meaning it can potentially be used to write malicious code or conduct cyber attacks. OpenAI says it has safeguards in place, but regulators and security researchers are deeply sceptical. This is the biggest AI milestone claim ever made — whether it's real or marketing hype, it's reshaping how governments, businesses, and investors think about the technology.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini 3.8 Flash — claims it matches rivals at lower cost
stories.why_it_matters: Google fired back this week with Gemini 3.8 Flash — a new model designed specifically to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic on coding tasks, but at a lower price point. Google is explicitly positioning this as the 'best value' AI model: same performance as rivals, cheaper to run. For developers and businesses choosing which AI to build products on, cost matters enormously. This is good news for GOOG holders — Google isn't ceding the AI race, it's competing hard on price as well as capability.

stories.title: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok all went down simultaneously
stories.why_it_matters: In a remarkable coincidence — or possibly something more concerning — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok all experienced outages on the same day this week, leaving thousands of users unable to access AI tools they now depend on for work. The outages highlighted just how centralised and fragile the AI infrastructure underpinning the global economy is becoming. When these services go down, it's not just an inconvenience — businesses lose productivity in real time. It's a reminder that 'cloud AI dependency' is a real risk for companies and investors.

stories.title: iOS 27 may let users swap ChatGPT for Gemini or Claude in Apple Intelligence
stories.why_it_matters: Apple is reportedly working on letting iPhone users in iOS 27 choose which AI brain powers Siri and Apple Intelligence — instead of being locked into ChatGPT, you could swap it for Google's Gemini or Anthropic's Claude. This is significant because it turns Apple's 1 billion+ iPhone users into a massive battleground for AI providers. For Google (GOOG), getting Gemini onto iPhones as the default assistant could be worth billions in future revenue — and it's exactly the kind of distribution advantage that makes Google's AI play so compelling long-term.

sport.summary: Round 27 NRL is underway — the Dolphins edged the Titans in a controversy-filled game on the Gold Coast tonight, the Broncos thumped the Bulldogs last night, and the Rabbitohs put 50 on the Roosters tonight. AFL finals teams are named with some big selection calls.

stories.title: Dolphins beat Titans 24-20 in fiery, controversy-filled Gold Coast clash
stories.why_it_matters: Right in your backyard — the Dolphins defeated the Gold Coast Titans 24-20 at Cbus Super Stadium tonight in what Fox Sports called a 'controversy-filled' match. An NRL great reportedly 'erupted' at a 'shocking decision' from the referee, and a Titans player received a standing ovation for being sin-binned in a fiery finish. With finals implications mounting in Round 27, every result counts.

stories.title: Broncos thump Bulldogs 34-20 at Accor Stadium
stories.why_it_matters: Brisbane Broncos had a comfortable 34-20 win over the Canterbury Bulldogs at Accor Stadium Thursday night. The Broncos continue to push for a strong finals position heading into the business end of the season.

stories.title: Rabbitohs thrash Roosters 50-20 in Friday night blockbuster
stories.why_it_matters: South Sydney Rabbitohs put up a massive 50-20 scoreline against the Sydney Roosters at Allianz Stadium on Friday night — a massive statement win. Scoring 50 points in a finals-relevant match is extraordinary and announces the Rabbitohs as genuine contenders heading into the final weeks of the regular season.

stories.title: AFL Finals teams named — Cats' selection shock, Swans' big call
stories.why_it_matters: AFL Finals team selections are in and there are some big calls — Geelong Cats have made a 'selection shock', the Blues have a blow with an injured player out, and the Sydney Swans have made a significant inclusion. With finals footy kicking off, every selection decision is magnified. The article doesn't detail all names, but the Cats' surprise drop/inclusion is the headline talking point heading into the weekend.
